article.title: Transform the Democratic Party
article.author: Alan Minsky
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Can the Democratic Party become a genuinely progressive, pro-working-class political force? Or is it, as many on the American left have long argued, the place where progressive movements go to die? Alan Minsky, executive director of Progressive Democrats of America (PDA), came to Left Coast Forum 2026 with a provocative answer: The Democratic Party can be transformed, but only if progressives organize to take control of it. Speaking at Cal State Los Angeles on October 4, Minsky challenged an audience of left activists to reconsider their relationship with electoral politics, particularly their longstanding frustration with the Democratic Party. A lifelong socialist and member of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Minsky was hardly offering an unqualified defense of the Democratic establishment. "There's nobody in this room who has more animus towards moderate Democrats than I do," he declared. Nevertheless, he argued that the Democratic Party remains the only viable political vehicle capable of defeating what he considers the growing threat of American fascism. The challenge, he insisted, is not to accommodate the party's centrist leadership but to replace it. The Two-Party Trap Minsky began by acknowledging something many progressives find deeply frustrating: America's electoral system has become increasingly hostile to third parties. Drawing on his experience as co-creator of the Ralph Nader Radio Hour , he discussed Nader's 2000 presidential campaign and the barriers that independent candidates have confronted since Ross Perot's surprisingly successful 1992 run. The problem, Minsky argued, is structural. Ballot-access requirements, campaign financing, and winner-take-all elections overwhelmingly favor the two established parties. But he identified an often-overlooked opportunity within that system: Democratic primaries. Unlike many European parliamentary parties, where leadership organizations exert considerable control over candidate selection, American primary elections allow voters to challenge incumbent politicians and party leadership. For Minsky, that opening is enormously consequential. Progressives do not necessarily need to build a new national party from scratch. They can compete for control of an existing one. "If we're in a two-party system and one of the parties genuinely [is] of the left," he argued, progressives would be remarkably close to controlling the government of the world's most powerful country. Related: Thomas Paine’s Common Sense for 2026: Progressives Must Transform the Democratic Party The Democrats Helped Create the Crisis Minsky's argument was accompanied by a blistering critique of the Democratic Party's recent history. He blamed the party's embrace of neoliberal economics for abandoning working-class Americans and creating fertile ground for Trump's political rise. Beginning in the late twentieth century, Democrats increasingly aligned themselves with corporate donors, financial interests, and market-oriented economic policies. The result, Minsky argued, was a political establishment increasingly disconnected from the material concerns of ordinary Americans. Working families struggled with declining economic security while wealth accumulated in the hands of investors and corporate elites. Minsky was especially critical of politicians who speak sympathetically about economic hardship while offering only limited reforms. He accused establishment Democrats of misleading voters about their commitment to working-class interests. "Of course, the Democratic Party is to blame for Trumpism," he said. "The Democratic Party absolutely betrayed and abandoned the working class." His critique extended beyond national politics to rural and small-town America, where Democrats have lost much of their former support. These communities, Minsky argued, have experienced economic decline without receiving a credible progressive alternative. The left should be able to reach these voters through a program addressing wages, economic security, and community survival. Instead, the party has too often allowed Republicans to monopolize working-class discontent. Beyond Affordability: Raise Working People's Wages Minsky emphasized that progressives need an economic program more ambitious than the familiar promise to make life affordable. He identified five major expenses undermining household finances: childcare, higher education, housing, health care, and high-interest debt. Reducing these costs is essential, he argued, but it addresses only half the problem. The other half is increasing what working people earn. "Democrats [are] running around the country and talking about affordability," he said. "Well, they're not talking about the one thing the working class really wants, which is higher salaries and higher wages." Minsky advocates a renewed commitment to the economic principles associated with Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal, updated for contemporary circumstances. He points to prosperous democracies that combine market economies with strong labor protections, public services, and government responsibility for economic security. His proposed 21st Century Economic Bill of Rights would guarantee access to necessities such as health care, housing, education, employment, and retirement security. For Minsky, these policies are not merely desirable reforms. They offer the foundation for a new political majority capable of rebuilding democratic institutions. A Green Party Challenge One of the afternoon's most revealing exchanges came when Michael Feinstein, a longtime Green Party organizer who said he had helped establish the party in the United States, challenged Minsky's dismissal of independent electoral organizing. Feinstein objected to Minsky's suggestion that left-wing third parties merely siphon votes from Democrats. Green voters, he explained, do not believe their votes belong to the Democratic Party in the first place. Many would otherwise abstain from voting, while others consciously support independent politics because they regard both major parties as responsible for the country's present condition. He also challenged Minsky's skepticism toward multiparty democracy. Rather than demanding that progressives join the Democrats, Feinstein argued, the left should work to change electoral rules through ranked-choice voting and proportional representation. Such reforms could allow multiple progressive parties to compete without automatically benefiting conservative candidates. The exchange exposed a genuine strategic division. For Feinstein, building an independent political alternative is itself an essential part of transforming American democracy. For Minsky, the urgency of defeating authoritarianism makes organizing within the Democratic Party the more practical and immediate strategy. Yet their disagreement was not absolute. Minsky acknowledged the value of Green Party policies and expressed support for electoral reforms, even while questioning whether they should be the central focus of progressive organizing. He also conceded that a sufficiently powerful independent movement could influence a transformed Democratic Party from outside. "I just think we need to find a way to have a unified left right now and not work against each other," he said. How Progressives Can Take Control Asked by another audience member how progressives could actually transform the Democratic Party, Minsky outlined two interconnected approaches. First, progressives must organize within the party's existing institutions, seeking influence over local organizations, state parties, national committees, and the rules governing electoral contests. Second, they must win primary elections, replacing establishment politicians with candidates committed to working-class economic policies. These efforts must reinforce one another. Progressive victories in primary elections can alter the direction of the party's elected leadership, while changes to internal party structures can make future progressive campaigns more competitive. Minsky also emphasized the importance of coordinated electoral organizing. Electing a few progressive members of Congress, he argued, is insufficient when meaningful legislative power requires a governing majority. "You got to get to 218," he observed, referring to the number of seats needed for a majority in the House of Representatives. Progressive organizations must therefore think beyond isolated victories and develop the capacity to win power nationally. Democracy Under a Stress Test Hovering over the discussion was Minsky's concern that the American constitutional system faces an extraordinary challenge. He described the 2026 midterm elections as a potential turning point in whether democratic institutions can withstand authoritarian pressure. Minsky argued that Americans must organize to defeat Republican candidates while continuing to challenge establishment Democrats within their own party. Importantly, he acknowledged that his strategy depends on the continued viability of democratic elections. If electoral outcomes cease to be respected, he suggested, the left may need to reconsider its political methods altogether. That possibility gave the discussion its particular urgency. From Resistance to Political Power Minsky's presentation reflected the central theme of Left Coast Forum 2026: "Building Power in an Age of Crisis: From Resistance to Reconstruction." His message was that opposition to authoritarianism cannot remain simply an exercise in protest. Movements must develop the organizational strength to win elections, enact legislation, and fundamentally reshape the economy. The discussion also demonstrated that progressives remain deeply divided about the best path forward. Some see the Democratic Party as an indispensable instrument for building political power. Others regard it as an obstacle that must ultimately be replaced. Minsky does not dismiss the party's failures. Indeed, he considers those failures central to explaining the country's current political crisis. But he believes the possibility of transforming the Democratic Party remains real, and that the opportunity must be seized before it disappears. The challenge he left with the audience was not simply whether progressives could win more elections. It was whether the American left could build a political movement strong enough to govern—and deliver the fundamental changes that ordinary Americans have been waiting for.
